A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DeCaFlow and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Despite extensive reorganization, corresponding methods, proofs, experiments, and results can be reliably matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic ablations, semi-synthetic Sachs and Ecoli70 experiments, and a law-school fairness study, with additional results in Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports revised results, an additional encoder-factorization ablation, and computational timing measurements.

M1.justification: The encoder changes from conditioning each confounder only on its children (v1 Eq. 5) to including parents of children and dependencies between latent confounders (v2 Eqs. 3 and 60). This changes the modeled posterior. The appendix counterfactual algorithm also replaces a posterior-mean plug-in with posterior sampling (v1 Algorithm 4 versus v2 Algorithm 5), aligning it with the main-text sampling description.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic linear/nonlinear settings, additive/nonadditive Sachs and Ecoli70 settings, and law-school Decile3 prediction task. The new factorization ablation and timing study reuse existing coverage. The napkin graph is a theoretical illustration, not an added empirical benchmark.

E2.justification: The named comparator sets remain unchanged. However, the law-school comparison models are revised: v1 Appendix B.5 specifies generalized linear predictors, whereas v2 Appendix B.6 uses gradient-boosted trees throughout, including for Fair K and Fair Add. Newly discussed confounded CGMs are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The law-school experiment changes its common downstream predictor family from generalized linear models to gradient-boosted trees. v2 also introduces a CPU timing protocol using 20,000 training samples and 2,500 inference samples. The newly stated 25,000-sample datasets and 80/10/10 splits are additional disclosures, not established changes to previously specified splits.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix B.3 and Figure 19 add an Ecoli70 ablation comparing children-only and expanded posterior factorizations, testing the benefit of modeling dependencies induced by colliders. Existing proxy-count, latent-dimensionality, encoder-selection, and KL-regularization ablations, together with analyses of unconfounded and unidentifiable effects, are retained.

E5.justification: New timing Tables 7–8 report means and standard deviations over 100 training epochs and seven or three inference interventions. Existing causal-error experiments retain five-run aggregation, 95% confidence intervals, and Mann–Whitney testing. The PDFs do not establish increased seed or run counts for those retained experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 2–6 replace numerous DeCaFlow results. For example, Sachs ATE error multiplied by 100 changes from 17.89 to 4.49 in the additive setting and from 3.26 to 5.16 in the nonadditive setting. Table 1 changes DeCaFlow RMSE from 1.652 to 1.604 and MMD from 0.0018 to 0.0054 under the revised predictor family. These are reported result changes, not uniform same-setting gains. Factorization-ablation and timing results are also added.

T1.justification: Building on v1's adjustment/proxy results and existing front-door example, v2 adds general do-calculus composition corollaries, a hedge definition and supporting argument in Appendix A.2, and a napkin-graph derivation in Appendix A.2.5. It also extends the do-calculus formulation to counterfactual estimation. The original proxy-identifiability and twin-SCM proofs are largely retained.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion redefine the advertised guarantee around queries reducible by do-calculus to observational or proxy-identifiable quantities, extending v1's adjustment-set/proxy formulation. The introduction also replaces v1's first-CGM framing with positioning DeCaFlow as a scalable, continuous-variable complement to existing approaches for hidden confounding.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly states that its proxy conditions are sufficient, so their failure need not imply unidentifiability; v1 Appendix A.2.2 gives a stronger failure interpretation. v2 adds explanations of collider-induced posterior dependence and removes v1's explicit conjecture about disentangling the remaining exogenous variables. The completeness and discrete-variable limitations are retained.

D1.justification: New Appendices B.5.3–B.5.4 and C substantially expand reproducibility information: hyperparameter-search choices, example network sizes and parameter count, dataset sizes and splits, optimization practices, CPU hardware, timing details, KL warm-up pseudocode, and structural masks. Most are newly disclosed details rather than demonstrated experimental changes. Code release remains promised upon acceptance.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands discussion of Neural Causal Models, modular causal generative models, and the previously cited bijective causal models. It adds proximal bridge-function estimators and critiques of latent-confounder approaches, including D'Amour's work. This changes the research positioning from a broad gap between existing approaches to explicit comparisons with prior confounded CGMs.

P1.justification: The abstract and much of the main exposition are rewritten. Related work moves into the introduction; background, problem formulation, and method are reorganized; theory is presented through inherited properties and query estimation; and practical guidance and limitations are redistributed. The appendices are reorganized around a new implementation section.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. v2 replaces the simple architecture sketch with detailed computations, adds architecture and sampling diagrams, a factorization-ablation plot, and timing tables. The fairness figure contracts from five predictor rows to two while Table 1 retains all methods. Figure 19 also introduces a caption/text overlap.

improvement.justification: v2 better specifies posterior dependencies and counterfactual sampling, adds a relevant ablation, and supplies previously missing implementation details. Its expanded discussion of existing confounded CGMs also improves assessment of the contribution. These gains are tempered by new variable inconsistencies in the napkin derivation, notably Eqs. 45 and 51–54, and an unchanged 98%/11% fairness summary in Appendix B.6 that no longer matches Table 1. The net quality gain is therefore limited.
